opus-5.5.text:
I think the timing came from a convergence of several things. For a long time, people in robotics knew the dream: a general-purpose robot that can work in homes, factories, shops. But the technology stack simply wasn't ready. Around 2022 and 2023, when large language models and vision-language models suddenly showed real generalization, it became clear to me that the "brain" side of the problem, understanding instructions, reasoning about tasks, recognizing objects in open environments, had taken a huge leap. What was missing was the body, and the ability to act in the physical world.

My own research for years had been on 3D vision, object manipulation, and simulation, especially how to get robots to grasp and manipulate objects they've never seen before. So I could see that the pieces were finally lining up: better perception, better foundation models, much cheaper and more capable hardware thanks to supply chains for electric vehicles and consumer electronics, and simulation and synthetic data that could address the data shortage in robotics.

There was also a sense of urgency. Whenever a technological window opens, it doesn't stay open forever. If you wait until everything is clear, the opportunity has already been taken. I believed embodied intelligence would be the next major frontier after large models, because intelligence that only lives on a screen can't truly change physical labor, elderly care, or manufacturing. Someone had to push it from the lab to the real world, and I felt that researchers who understood both the algorithms and the robotics had a responsibility to do it now, not five years later.

Finally, the data problem convinced me that we had to start early. Unlike language models, robots don't have an internet's worth of data. You need to build the data pipeline, the simulation system, and the hardware together, and that takes time to accumulate. The earlier you start, the bigger your advantage. That's why I felt we couldn't wait.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics data is scarce and calls for building data pipelines, simulation, and hardware, but does not state that the needed data must come from real-world physical interaction.

r002.rationale: It connects embodied intelligence to physical labor, elderly care, and manufacturing, then says it should be pushed into the real world now rather than five years later.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from a sense of timing more than anything else. I had been working on 3D vision and robot learning for years, and for most of that time the field moved in small steps. Then around 2022, 2023, several things lined up at once. Large language models showed that scaling data and compute could produce general capability, not just narrow skills. Simulation got good enough that we could generate robot data at a volume the physical world could never give us. And hardware, especially dexterous hands and affordable arms, finally became something a lab could actually buy and iterate on.

When you see three curves bending upward together, you don't wait. I kept asking myself: if general-purpose robots are going to happen in this decade, who is going to build the brain for them? If we in academia only published papers, we would be describing the future rather than making it. So I felt we had to put a real system into the physical world, with real users, and let reality teach us what the papers couldn't.

There was also a more personal reason. Vision research had become very crowded, and a lot of it was about squeezing out another percentage point on a benchmark. Embodied intelligence was the opposite. Nothing worked yet. A robot that could reliably grasp an unseen object in a messy kitchen was still a hard problem. That gap between what we could already do in pixels and what we could not do in the world, that was where I wanted to spend my time. And I believed if we didn't start right then, we would be two or three years behind the people who did.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation can generate robot data and that reality can teach what papers cannot, but it does not clearly state that developing physical-world intelligence requires data from real-world physical interaction.

r002.rationale: The response argues that general-purpose robots and difficult real-world tasks such as grasping unseen objects make embodied intelligence urgent, and says they had to start then to avoid falling behind.

astra-6.text:
I felt we needed to start immediately because embodied intelligence requires us to bring perception, decision-making, and action together in the physical world. A system has to do more than recognize an object or describe a task—it has to act, observe what happens, and adjust when things don’t go as expected.

That creates a long development cycle. We need to build systems, test them in real environments, learn from failures, and use those experiences to improve them. We can’t wait until every individual technology is mature before beginning that process. Starting now is how we discover which problems actually matter and what we still need to solve.

r001.rationale: The response describes acting and observing in the physical world, testing in real environments, and using the resulting experiences to improve systems.

r002.rationale: It argues for starting immediately because development takes a long cycle, but does not say that the need for embodied intelligence across hands-on applications justifies beginning now.

sol-6.1.text:
I felt we needed to start immediately because embodied intelligence requires us to solve problems that don’t appear when AI only processes information on a screen. A robot has to perceive its surroundings, understand what matters, and act—and then deal with the consequences of that action. Those capabilities have to work together in the physical world, where conditions are constantly changing.

There’s also a practical reason to begin early: collecting experience in the real world takes time. You need to build systems, test them, learn why they fail, and improve them. You can’t assume that once an AI model becomes powerful enough, all of those physical challenges will disappear. So I saw embodied intelligence as a long-term effort that we needed to start now.

r001.rationale: It says real-world experience must be collected by building systems, testing them, and learning from failures, communicating the need to learn through physical-world interaction.

r002.rationale: It explains that robots must perceive and act in changing physical conditions, then says this long-term effort needed to start immediately.
